Kindergarten · Unit K-A

Pushes and Pulls

How can a push or pull change how something moves?

Pushes and pulls are how we make things move. You will try pushing and pulling objects to start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn them, find out how strength and direction change what happens, and design something that changes motion safely.

In this lesson

  1. Pushes and pulls start, stop, and change motion
  2. Strength and direction matter
  3. We can design things to change motion safely
  4. Try it at home
  5. Check yourself
  6. Play: Push-Pull Test Track

What is new. You may have compared things in K2.0 or Unit 0. This lesson is your first fair test with pushes and stoppers. A fair test changes one thing and keeps everything else the same. A stopper is something that slows or stops a moving car.

A push sends something away from you. A pull brings it toward you.

Look for these tags: Analogy, Diagram, Try it, Data, Real world

Concept 1

Pushes and pulls start, stop, and change motion

A push or pull can make an object start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, or turn.

Analogy

Motion means moving.

A child on a swing.

“A push starts me. A hand stops me.”

Diagram

Look at the arrows. An arrow shows which way a push or pull goes.

“The arrow shows the push or pull.”

Try it

Guess first: If you tap a toy car gently, will it go far or not far?

What you need: one toy car, a flat floor or table, a line of tape.

Do: Put the car on the tape line. Give it a gentle push. Watch where it stops. Now roll it back, push again, and this time use your hand to stop it before it goes far.

Look for: The car did not start by itself. Your push made it go. Your hand made it stop.

What it shows: A push can start motion, and a push from your hand can also stop it.

Safety: Keep small cars away from mouths. Roll on the floor, not near stairs.

“Make it go. Make it stop.”

Real world

Pull a sled up a snowy hill. Push a door open.

“You pull a sled up the hill. You push a door open.”

Concept 2

Strength and direction matter

A stronger push or a different direction can change how far or where an object goes.

Try it

Guess first: Will a strong blow move a cotton ball farther than a soft blow?

What you need:

  • one cotton ball
  • a table
  • a strip of tape about 30 centimeters (12 inches) long

Do: Set the cotton ball on the table. Blow gently from the side, then blow harder. Mark where it stops each time.

Look for: Did the cotton ball move farther with the strong blow?

What it shows: A stronger blow can make an object go farther.

Safety: Do not put the cotton ball near your mouth or nose. Never suck on a straw. Cotton balls are a choking hazard for small children.

“Soft blow. Strong blow. Which goes farther?”

Data

Here is how far the car rolled (example data).

“Soft push: the car rolled 2 floor tiles, about 60 centimeters (2 feet). Strong push: 6 floor tiles, about 180 centimeters (6 feet).”

Soft push
Strong push

One square is one floor tile. A floor tile is about 30 centimeters (1 foot).

Real world

Wind pushes a sailboat. A snowplow pushes snow.

“Wind can push a sailboat on the Great Lakes.”

Concept 3

We can design things to change motion safely

A good design can slow, stop, or turn motion on purpose.

A stopper is anything that slows or stops a rolling car.

Diagram

Look at the ramp and the stopper.

  • Draw
  • Build
  • Test
Try it

Guess first: Will your stopper keep the car from rolling past the line? Draw it first.

What you need:

  • toy car
  • a ramp (a book with a piece of cardboard leaning on it)
  • tape for the finish line
  • a piece of foam, a paper cup, or a cardboard block

Do: Tape a finish line on the floor. Roll the car down the ramp with no stopper to see where it goes. Then build a stopper and put it on the line. Roll the car again. Did the car stop before the line?

Look for: A soft stopper (foam) can slow the car gently. A hard one can make it bounce back. Change one thing and test again.

What it shows: A design is an idea you test. If the car rolls past, the design can be fixed.

Safety: Keep small stoppers and cars out of mouths. Wipe up any spills so no one slips.

“Can your block stop the car?”

Data

Here is what happened when we tested two stoppers 3 times (example data).

“Foam stopped it 3 times out of 3. Cardboard stopped it 1 time out of 3.”

Foam✓✓✓
Cardboard✓○○

A check means the car stopped before the line. A circle means it did not.

Real world

A gate keeps a rolling ball away from the street.

“A gate can stop a ball before it rolls toward the street.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Safe Stopper Design. Problem: a toy car rolls too far. You sketch, build, and test two stoppers or ramp ends. Test each design 3 times, then pick the better one by looking at what your tests showed.

Try it

What you need

  • toy car or spool
  • cardboard ramp
  • tape
  • a piece of foam
  • paper cup
  • a sticker or a small piece of tape to mark each stop
  • paper strips about 30 centimeters (12 inches) long, or graph paper

Safety: Keep small cars and stoppers away from mouths, and clean up spills so no one slips.

What you do

Station 1, Pushes (about 10 minutes). Roll a toy car with a soft push and a strong push. Put a sticker where each one stops. Count the floor tiles. Each tile is about 30 centimeters (1 foot) long. Which push went farther?

Station 2, Safe Stopper (about 20 minutes). Draw a ramp and a stopper. Build two different stoppers (for example foam and cardboard). Roll the car 3 times at each and write one mark each time it stops before the line.

Look for: the stopper that stopped the car more times out of 3 tries. Say: “Foam stopped it ___ times. Cardboard stopped it ___ times.”

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence. Collecting your own data is best when you can.

If you cannot run the physical test, use this example data: soft push = 2 floor tiles (about 60 centimeters); strong push = 6 floor tiles (about 180 centimeters). Foam stopper stopped the car 3 out of 3 tries. Cardboard stopper stopped the car 1 out of 3 tries.

Near you:
  • Wind can push boats on the Great Lakes.
  • Snowplows push snow off the road.
  • Children sled down hills and use their feet or a barrier to stop.

Words to know

push
A push moves something away from where it is.
pull
A pull moves something toward you.
motion
Motion means moving.
force
A force is a push or a pull.
direction
Direction means which way.
strength
Strength means how hard.
speed
Speed means how fast.
design
To design is to plan and make something.
stopper
A stopper slows or stops a moving car.
fair test
A fair test changes one thing and keeps everything else the same.
data
Data is information we collect from tests.
Tutor notes: misconceptions and pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Objects stop because they run out of push.” Correct: another push or pull, such as rubbing or a barrier, can slow or stop motion.
  • “Only people push or pull.” Correct: wind, water, and gravity can also push or pull.
  • “A bigger push always gives the same result.” Correct: object shape, surface, and barriers matter too.
  • “A push is only with hands.” Correct: a push can be air, water, or another object.
  • “A pull moves something away from you.” Correct: a pull moves something toward you.
  • “One try is enough.” Correct: we repeat tests to be more sure.
  • “Changing many things makes a fair test.” Correct: a fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same.

Limits and cautions:

  • Friction is not named deeply; K-2 students only need to see slowing and stopping.
  • Gravity may come up as a pull. This is accurate but not required.
  • Repeat each test. One test is not enough.
  • Small parts need supervision.
  • Design choice: counting floor tiles or paper strips as K distance data. Count floor tiles or paper strips laid end to end as the distance unit. Use the same tile size or strip length for every test, and write that size on the data sheet.
